questions.q: How does Project 3 differ from Projects 1 and 2?
options: It gives a full click-by-click recipe
It uses no data
It gives a brief and hints, and you decide the reports, fields, and chart types
It is shorter than the others
questions.explain: Project 3 mirrors real work: an executive brief with minimal guidance, so the design decisions are yours.

questions.q: The annual team quota is $9.0M and $1.5M has been won this quarter. With an even quarterly quota of $2.25M, what is the remaining gap?
questions.explain: 2.25 minus 1.5 equals 0.75, so $0.75M remains to be closed this quarter.

questions.q: Which requirement in the brief most clearly requires combining objects?
options: Whether we are generating enough leads
Whether the pipeline reaches quota
Whether the dashboard fits on one page
Whether service problems are putting deals at risk
questions.explain: Service problems live on Cases, deals on Opportunities, and the two connect through the Account.

questions.q: Your pipeline report shows $21M closing this quarter for a team with a $2.25M quarterly quota. What should you do?
options: Publish it because bigger numbers impress executives
Treat the number as suspect and investigate filters, duplicates, or date ranges before using it
Round it down to fit
Delete the report
questions.explain: Sanity-check facts exist to catch implausible results, which often come from missing filters or duplicated rows.

questions.q: Why decide what would change the VP's mind before building a chart?
options: Charts cannot be built without a decision
Salesforce requires a documented decision
So every number on the page is one the VP could act on
It removes the need to reconcile
questions.explain: Executive dashboards earn their space by supporting decisions. Numbers nobody can act on add noise.
